item.title: On Writing #3
item.description:
Periodically I like to gather various observations about writing, and share my perspective. Last time was in honor of my trip to Inkhaven. This time will be in honor of the announcement of Inkhaven #3, which I encourage everyone to apply to. I doubt I will be able to usefully be an advisor, but you never know.

This is not the ‘here is my core process’ post, although there are hints throughout as there always are. I’ll do that at some point.

Previously in series: On Writing #1, On Writing #2.

Table of Contents

  1. You Still Got It.
  2. How Scott Sumner Writes.
  3. How Scott Alexander Writes.
  4. How Jasmine Sun Writes.
  5. How Various Famous Writers Write.
  6. How Nabeel Qureshi Defines Great Writing.
  7. Quickly, There’s No Time.
  8. If At First.
  9. Writers Have A Harder Time Influencing, But It Can Still Be Done.
  10. It’s Not (Only) The Incentives, It’s (Also) You.
  11. Beware The Fetish of the Desk.
  12. How Orson Scott Card Writes.
  13. Doing The Math Is Fun And Supererogatory.
  14. Brevity is the Soul of Wit.

You Still Got It

I used to be like this more often, constantly doubting first if I had it at all, then later if I still got it, then finally if I’ll blow it.

Hitting post used to be absolutely terrifying, every time.

It’s no longer routine for me to freak out but I’m not zero percent like this now:

Dean W. Ball: By the way if you are a young writer and not routinely freaking out about “whether you still got it” you aren’t doing it right. That anxiety is what drives you forward.

Anton Leicht: i don’t know anyone whose writing I love whose work isn’t the product of defying ‘it’s so over, i’m washed, no one will ever read anything else i write again’ over and over again

Dean W. Ball: yes, Beethoven spoke of this too

Nathan Lambert (fixed it?): By the way if you are a writer and not routinely freaking out about “whether you still got it” you aren’t doing it right. That anxiety is what drives you forward.

Dean W. Ball: Agreed! But I figure all the older writers know this :)

Andy Masley: Literally every time I sit down with a new thing

Dean W. Ball: Almost literally every week I wake up and say to myself “everything good you’ve ever written is behind you, and it wasn’t even ever that good and now you have no more juice” and then I sit down to write

What about me?

I worry that I’ve had or used all my good ideas, that I’ll be repeating myself.

I worry that I won’t recapture the magic that goes into a really great post.

I worry that I missed the key windows of time to say the important things.

I worry I’m getting too old and my brain is slowly not working right anymore.

I worry I’m going to start making big mistakes and look like an idiot.

My real anxiety these days comes not from ‘I don’t got it’ but from ‘I could blow it.’ It stems from the opportunity, from the stakes of the games I’m trying to play.

Whereas I guess if I ‘don’t have it’ then there’d really be nothing to sweat, you know?

The worries mostly apply to me for my ‘effort posts,’ where I’m trying to assemble a clear thesis and create something that will last. For roundups and weeklies, I don’t much worry about it. Those are more like ‘clocking in.’

I notice that most of the time, when I do really have something, I stop worrying.

I draw the parallel to being a competitor in Magic: The Gathering. I would worry I didn’t have it. When I was really clocked in I didn’t worry about not having it, I worried more about blowing the chance when I did have it. So it’s a similar pattern.

Is the anxiety actually useful? Does it drive you forward? To some extent yes. In order to write well you have to reinvent, to do something you haven’t done before, and you have to struggle and push through bad ideas and false starts and so on, and be intolerant of things that aren’t good enough or could be better.

But I don’t think it’s necessary, at least not for everyone. You just need something pushing you forward, some form of dread about not putting in every last bit of effort. You can be driven forward by opportunity or risk, rather than anxiety about ability, and I’m sure there are other similar tricks.

How Scott Sumner Writes

Scott Sumner looks at Virginia Woolf on writing advice, and offers a list of his own.

Scott Sumner:

  1. Do a lot of reading—that’s where ideas come from. Read in all sorts of fields, even fields you might assume to be useless, such as philosophy. But also try to be an expert in at least one field.
  2. Do a lot of writing, as writing helps one to think.
  3. Think of blogging as a form of conversation. When you converse with people, you presumably are aware of your audience. That should also be true of blogging—think about who you are writing for.
  4. Even a great novel or painting is a form of conversation, Artists are reacting to what other artists have done. A blogger just starting out should probably not be presenting grand theories of everything, rather one should start by reacting to what others are discussing.
  5. People complained that I often “bury the lede”. So, I guess you shouldn’t do that. Give people an idea of where you are going if you want them to stick with the post—at least until you have enough of a reputation that they can trust you to go somewhere interesting.
  6. Avoid a self-consciously literary style. Write as you’d speak.
  7. Ask yourself: Is it possible I’ll regret this? How might this post be misinterpreted? You might want to set it aside for a day, then reread before posting. When I do so, I often end up cutting out things that might have brought me grief.
  8. Personality flaws are exposed in blog posts, but writing also makes it easier to fix these flaws. Keep in mind that your critics are usually right (apart from trolls.) If a smart well-intentioned commenter says the post was unfair or mean-spirited, it usually is.
  9. Words don’t just have literal meanings, they have connotations. The term ‘ignorant’ doesn’t mean stupid, but it has come to have that implication. Don’t think to yourself, “I should not have to tell readers that just because I claim a certain politician is an idiot, doesn’t mean that I view his supporters as stupid.” You do have to say that, even though logic would suggest it’s unnecessary.

In other words, because people are stupid it is important to reassure them that you don’t view them as stupid.

I especially endorse #2, #5 (I’m working on it), #6 and the core of #9. You do not have to say it, but you do have to either say it or accept that the connotation is there. There is no universal law saying you have to disclaim every connotation you don’t fully endorse, but you do want to leave them there on purpose.

How Scott Alexander Writes

Scott Alexander offers a bunch of writing advice. Paraphrase summaries follow, then my reactions are nested.

  1. Avoid micro dishonesty. Don’t try to smuggle in your point, hide the weaknesses, go with the slightly misleading introduction, or pretend things turned out a way they didn’t. The readers will notice and it won’t work.
    1. Agreed. Scott Sumner’s point on integrity is similar.
  2. Avoid cliches, and treat them as opportunities to say a cool thing instead.
    1. Agreed when it would be cliche in the bad way, but not in the good way.
    2. That might sound unhelpful. What I mean is, don’t do the unfun straight man repetition thing, but playing around or using them like normal words is fine.
  3. Follow writing rules until you understand the real underlying bad thing, which makes you good enough to get away with breaking the rule. Give yourself particular rules to follow that match what you need to fix.
    1. Agreed, but don’t spend too long on that mountaintop.
  4. Untangle your sentences, just say the thing, unless you have a good reason.
    1. Agreed. Tangled is fine if and only if you know why you’re doing it.
  5. He’s against explainers.
    1. My rule is, only write an explainer if you would often use it as a link.
  6. The five paragraph essay is awful but the basic idea behind it is good.
    1. Yep. Tell ‘em what you’re gonna tell ‘em, tell ‘em, tell ‘em what you told ‘em.
    2. This is one I have to keep working on. I keep reminding myself, at least one of the opening and the closing needs to contain the central takeaways.
  7. Don’t write your blog about other blogs. Introduce new info or GTFO.
    1. It has to be something that works if they’ve read your sources.
    2. It also has to be something that works if they haven’t read your sources.
  8. Write brilliantly about anything, or decently about what people care about.
    1. Basically, yeah.
    2. As Scott says, most success will be from option two. Option one is harder.
  9. [A parable that one can interpret a lot of different ways.]
  10. There are tons of effort posts out there waiting to be written.
    1. I mean, sure.
  11. The true blogger finds unexpected opportunities to start pointless but delightful conflicts.
    1. Strongly agree. Go forth and find them. It’s like abstract mathematics, in that you think it’s all pointless, and it works better if you don’t worry about the point, but it then turns out there was a point after all.
  12. The point of poetry is that restrictions breed creativity, so you can strike gold.
    1. Maybe. I dunno. I don’t really get it.
  13. You need to always buy enough runway to keep reader attention. Start strong.
    1. Strongly agree, in most situations.
    2. Notice that sometimes you actually have quite a lot of runway. Use it.
    3. Also notice that once you’re profitable, you can keep going indefinitely.
    4. Well, kinda. I test that theory a lot.
  14. You need conflict and mystery but it can be pretty much anything.
    1. I think of it as interest or curiosity. Probably mostly the same idea.
  15. Give readers things they can’t trivially generate from a prompt.
    1. Whenever possible, this is a good idea. Need it somewhere.
    2. But also, they mostly won’t bother to run the prompt.
    3. Often you need it to have been said as a reference point.
  16. Just say the thing you want to say.
    1. Yep.

How Jasmine Sun Writes

She does her homework.

Jasmine Sun: When you become a writer, here is one of the first things you will discover: with about a month of dedicated effort, you can go from knowing nothing about a topic to being able to present fluently and converse with experts. The beginning will be painful.

You will sound stupid for your first ten conversations, maybe fifty.

At first jargon will look like gibberish, then it will be faintly recognizable, and then one day intelligible, like fog clearing from the hills; with every additional source you read, your story will reveal itself in greater fidelity and scope. “If you do everything, you’ll win,” as Robert Caro says.

There is a comforting if-then determinism to Caro’s advice: research persistence is rewarded, success is guaranteed. You chip away at your hypothesis until something more interesting is revealed: an essay is a failure if you go in with an outline and it emerges the same shape. The world is both unimaginably intricate and more knowable than it looks.

Fifty conversations or interviews about a topic seems like a lifetime to me. That’s a very different alien mode of being and way of learning. I don’t know that I’ve ever even done two. But Jasmine is doing a very different kind of investigative or exploratory journalism, based largely on interviews. Whereas I depend on learning from what is written.

It seems so weird to impose on people and ask them to be interviewed, especially when Claude is right there, even though I get asked and I often say yes. I should go to the sources more often.

Jasmine is constantly taking notes about everything. On the margin that has to be right, yet I find myself unmotivated to do it.

Another alien thing to me is a work in progress ‘living in your head’ like this:

Jasmine Sun: At some point in every writing project, it stops living in the Google Doc and starts living in your mind. Everything else you see and hear gets filtered through the frame of the essay.

To me, to the extent work lives in my head, that is before you open the doc, not during or after. There are also a bunch more things she talks about in the full essay.

How Various Famous Writers Write

Useful pieces of writing advice from several writers, from 2010.

Elmore Leonard is all about what stupid things not to do: Never open with weather, avoid prologues, always use “said” for dialogue without adverbs, almost no exclamation points, no ‘suddenly’ or ‘all hell broke loose,’ minimal regional dialect, no detailed character descriptions, avoid long place and thing details, leave out things readers skip. If it sounds like writing, rewrite it.

Diana Athill says read it aloud to yourself, have no inessential words, be highly suspicious of your darlings.

Margaret Atwood focuses on physical tools like pencils and a thesaurus that I would say you don’t need anymore. She also steps back to earlier points if something went awry, does back exercises and hold the reader’s attention and has others look with fresh eyes.

There’s a bunch more. The biggest takeaway is they have some overlaps but are all different, and often very personal things that won’t generalize. The only commonality is ‘write.’

How Nabeel Qureshi Defines Great Writing

What makes text into great art? Nabeel Qureshi says good text is surprising and also it echoes over layers doing multiple things at once, it makes you think, it changes what it means as you read it. Great writing contains themes and layers most readers never notice. It has depth that is impossible to paraphrase, contains mysteries and is open to different interpretations.

I would say these are some of the things that make art great, and yes for now we do not know how to get AI to do this. Then again, I don’t know how to create ‘great art’ either, and have yet to produce what I consider even a short passable work of fiction or poetry.

Quickly, There’s No Time

Eukaryote points out that quick take posts are often about interesting things that require little context. This can be a lot more important than all the details and editing you pour into your effort posts.

In particular I’d note that having a great hook is a lot of what gets one to go viral and get posted to places like Hacker News, and that virality is how you get your hits until you’ve built up a big subscription base.

You can of course do even better by producing the cool concept post and then editing it within an inch of its life, as in ‘taking the time to write a shorter letter.’

Some, but far from all, of my historically successful posts did that.

If At First

Is it better to write quickly and revise, or write slowly and get it right the first time?

g a b y: the most liberating thing in the world is realizing you can just write it bad. you can write it bad and make it good later. does everyone know about this??????

Nate Silver: I write like shit sometimes but actually bad advice, writing bad and revising takes longer than chilling out and writing well once you’re good and ready.

Kyle Bown: I think it depends greatly on the KIND of writing you’re doing. I find if I’m writing a script, I need to just get the first draft out. There’s so many moving pieces to telling a story in that format that editing is necessary. An article or think piece is better to do it the first time.

Here is another case of Nate Silver pushing back against ‘write the first draft quick.’

If you are struggling to write something, could it be you don’t know what you think? That is indeed my experience.

Paul Sax: Excellent advice for avoiding writer’s block. Just get the draft down as fast as possible. Revise later.

Nate Silver: Not meaning to be critical. This will work great for some people. I just think there’s very wide variation among writers about whether you do your “thinking on the page” vs. “thinking in your head”.

I’m on the extreme opposite end where like the first two drafts are in my head, maybe with a little bit of outlining or a few snippets written down (certainly for longer pieces). Not inherently good or bad, but that’s how my brain works for whatever reason.

So for me, when I’m struggling to write, it’s often because I haven’t done enough reading or given myself enough time to let ideas marinate. Just “getting something down on the page” can sometimes make that worse especially if you grow attached to your copy.

I largely think on the page, as I write. Which means I often start writing before I know what I want to say. It also means I would never write a passage in order to have an early version, or move on from a paragraph that I know is not good enough. If it is not good enough, I am not done thinking. I am not ready to move on.

I also think that part of why my process works so quickly is that I don’t train myself that it is okay to write these ‘vomit drafts.’ If you’re willing to do that, you’re committing to rewrites.

Then again, I never write fiction. If I wrote fiction, I could totally see doing what famed Simpsons writer Swartzwelder says to do, writing filler dialogue and jokes to have a first draft, so you know what you are looking at, and then fill in from there. Maybe that’s a good idea.

It’s fine to write badly, so long as you notice, as an exercise, but then you need to throw most of it out and start over. You can keep actively good bits.

The key difference I have is, for my purposes writing nonfiction, I find that trying to revise bad writing is way harder than writing well in the first place. If I realize something is bad I’m inclined to entirely start over. In fiction perhaps it does not work that way? I’m not sure.

None of this gets you out of editing. Editing starts with good and makes it great.

Writers Have A Harder Time Influencing, But It Can Still Be Done

Noah Smith is worried that bloggers are losing influence.

Part of this is that we are in a populist era, when the right is led by Trump who acts on instincts built from TV and real estate and zero sum games, and listens to whoever talked to him last, and the left is largely insular and only listens inside its echo chamber. So you can’t much influence either.

I would respond that yes this makes it harder, but you can still influence both.

Dean Ball went straight to the White House and has had strong influence on policy. When the time comes to grope around for those instincts, or for whoever talks to Trump last to talk to him last, someone is still puppeteering that, to a large degree. I’ve had various doors opened for me as well.

You can still drive the online conversation. There are those in the administration very aware of sentiments on Substack and Twitter. Keep posting. But do watch framing. You can turn the administration against you if you provoke the wrong adversarial frame.

On the left, you have the moderates who listen to the intellectuals more than ever, and no they don’t purely fold to the left. As for the harder left like Mamdani, you still see him for example knowing his YIMBY facts. These people do sometimes listen. Other times not so much directly, and absolutely they can be off in their own world, but part of the job is to make sure that world doesn’t end up in charge. So there’s at least that.

It’s Not (Only) The Incentives, It’s (Also) You

Smith’s second concern is that Substack is a newsletter platform that rewards those who maximize subscribers, so you end up isolated and not in dialogue with other bloggers and thinkers. There’s no republic of letters.

My response is a mix of ‘it’s not the incentives, it’s you’ plus skill issue. Noah Smith has over 300k subscribers. He doesn’t have to be maximizing revenue. I have a lot less subscribers, largely because I don’t maximize, because I recognize that the impact is on a power law, by bringing key things to the key people who will act on that.

I do worry about the ‘silo effect,’ where you do better if you stay in your lane. I want to write about games more, or other fun things, but that gets punished. I pay some price for the tangents I do insist upon.

I find the silo problem even worse on Twitter or other social media than Substack. If you’re giving me 50% Tweets I want and 50% Tweets I don’t want, then that’s no good, because the cost of evaluating a Tweet is high relative to the cost of full consumption. Whereas if you give me 50% articles or books I want, and 50% that I don’t, that’s great. You can totally spam my inbox with the other half, because I spend one minute discarding the bad things and 1 hour consuming the good thing. It’s only a problem if the bad things fool you into investing a lot of time.

Smith’s third concern is that AI is hurting our attention spans, causing more skimming versus less reading, and generating a lot of its own posts. Here I worry less.

I strongly disagree with him that the AI-written articles are already good. You can use Claude to generate serviceable text if the goal is an infodump and you also do a bunch of work, if you want. It’s at best serviceable and like Noah’s example would likely show up at ~50% AI on Pangram. At least for now. Such text plays somewhat better to audiences who don’t yet have much AI writing exposure.

Matt Yglesias notes he took a pay cut and gave up his Bloomberg Opinion column to write in The New York Times in order to reach the audience only NYT can provide. As someone who did successfully get one piece into NYT, I can say the same except at even higher abstraction. I wrote that article in order to write future articles that would then get a key message across. The other advantage is I had a really great editor. It was a lot of work but also a joy to have someone who cared about making my work the best it can be.

Lulu Cheng Meservey charts new sales after various exposures. National outlets did little, substacks did relatively a lot.

This matched my own experience. I got into The New York Times once and if I showed you my subscriber graph you wouldn’t be able to notice that date at all. That doesn’t mean it isn’t impactful in other ways, especially in reaching a lot of otherwise hard to reach people who matter.

Beware The Fetish of the Desk

I am heavily on the pragmatist side in terms of your setup. You should indeed as Robert McFarlane says ‘beware the fetish of the desk’ and not worry about getting the details right or keeping things straight or what not. If you find clutter is bothering you, fix it. If you don’t like your pencil, get a better pencil, and so on.

The exception is your computer and monitor setup. Invest in that, whether or not you are a writer. You want at least two monitors, with the central one being large. I use three 30-inch monitors, all three are fully used at all times, and if I did it over again I would have four but have decided it isn’t worth redoing everything to fix that.

I find that when forced to write without my setup, I am at least ~50% less productive. I’ve given myself a rule that I don’t try to write elsewhere, unless I am going to be in a place for an extended period. If so I try damn hard to get at least one good monitor.

Then again, there are plenty of writers who don’t need secondary screens, and are perfectly happy to write on laptops. For some forms I think this is fine, for others not.

How Orson Scott Card Writes

Orson Scott Card on how he expanded a short story into the full book Ender’s Game in a matter of weeks. He says he did almost no prep for the book, because his prep was his childhood, which he transferred directly onto Ender, and things like a trilogy of books about the Army of the Potomac which mapped onto the other commanders at battle school.

This resonated with me. I spent a long time thinking about related ideas, but once I decided to write the Moral Mazes sequence I mostly wrote it within a week, and a lot of my other key works that have held up well were written quickly.

Orson Scott Card also explains that when you get rejected as a writer, you should treat that the same way game designers treat such feedback. When they say something is wrong, they’re right, and they can often point towards it. When they tell you how to fix it, you can mostly ignore them, and should figure out yourself how to fix it.

Another note is that when you are rejected, the editor usually won’t even know why they are rejecting you, so they definitely can’t tell you the reason. Very true.

The last note is that editors are dramatically different before and after you sign a contract. Before you sign a contract, they’re usually not concentrating attention enough to be general intelligences and don’t know much. After you sign a contract, now they have a stake in the outcome, and if they are good at their job then they’re great and invaluable. My pitching experience has been extremely frustrating, but every time an editor actually focused on improving the writing it has been great.

Doing The Math Is Fun And Supererogatory

Roach-works notes that if you are writing speculative fiction and you get detailed, some of your readers will point out your details are wrong and be upset about this. So Roach’s advice is to not give specifics. The city is old, the sword is heavy.

To which Misha correctly responds, screw the haters, you can ignore them.

Misha is correct, if you are willing and able. It is much better to make some mistakes than to keep everything vague. However, keeping everything vague is also totally an option, if you do not want to do the research.

You can make mistakes. You don’t want to be making glaringly obvious mistakes, or have your economic values be off by orders of magnitude such that the whole thing makes no sense. And you may not need the details at all. If you want to tell a story that fundamentally doesn’t physically work, then it’s time for that heavy sword.

Brevity is the Soul of Wit

How long is too long? Asking for a friend (named Dean Ball).

Dean W. Ball: I just wrote a 5,300 word essay. Should I yeet it out as one long essay or split it into two parts? A normal essay on Hyperdimensional is 2.5-3k words. The risk to two parts is neither half can sustain itself without the other; the risk to one is obviously overwhelming readers.

Patrick McKenzie: The people who run the world mostly read, and people who read are not intimidated by pieces at their natural length. If the natural length is 5k words, ship 5k words.

Ben: The public yearns for longpost

Dean W. Ball: I’m kinda shocked

My take for posts that have a thesis, rather than being roundups:

You should only ever split an article into two small parts in places where the parts can stand on their own. If no one would ever want to link to or read Part 1 without Part 2, or Part 2 without Part 1, then you want to post it all at once, no matter the length.

That assumes you are on the internet, so you face no physical limitations. Except the Gmail clipping at ~102KB, but that ship sailed for me a while ago.

The reason The Sequences work so well is that while they form one large construction, you can link to or read each individual post on its own.

If you have a full book of content, then you have to split it into chapters, even if the chapters don’t stand on their own, but I would not consider that below 10k words, and would only seriously consider it around 20k, even if your normal length is 2k.

For roundups, I think it’s fine to split sooner, especially if that gives the sections better common themes. My new goal is non-AI roundups topping out around 5k.

So, while noting that everyone’s process is different and you need to find what works for you via experimentation, we’d better end here before we hit that mark.

item.title: The Reified Referent: How the Saturation View Values the Taste of Someone Who Does Not Exist
item.description:
TLDR

The Saturation View holds that a world of varied joys is better than a world of equal but identical joys. Elliott Thornley objected that no one benefits from this variety, and Will MacAskill answered that it is a claim about the pattern of value in the world, rather than about individuals' experiences. This post elaborates on Thornley's point and argues that a pattern that possibly no one ever experiences is not a valid moral category. Treating it as intrinsically valuable smuggles a fictional experiencer into the moral conversation.

I call this the reified referent: the mirror image of Carol J. Adams's absent referent. Where the absent referent hides a real being, the reified referent invents an unreal one.

There may be good instrumental arguments for variety, but we should reject the claim that a world can be made better by a change that no individual gains from. And if, like me, you care more about reducing suffering than increasing happiness, there may be a danger in valuing variety, since it can push toward widening the spectrum of valence, away from stability and perhaps tranquility.

Thanks to @KonradKozaczek and @Alistair Stewart for helpful comments on this post. 

My View on Saturationism's Main Claim

In The Saturation View, Will MacAskill, in work with Christian Tarsney, proposes that the value of an experience depends not only on its welfare but on how many relevantly similar experiences already exist. Near duplicates have diminishing marginal value. A world's value is a function of total welfare and of how widely that welfare is spread across the landscape of possible experience types. So Variety, a world of diverse excellent lives, beats Homogeneity, a world of equal welfare concentrated in identical copies of the single best life.

I think variety could have instrumental value: exploration, robustness, error correction, and hedging under moral uncertainty. Felt variety is valuable too: novelty, contrast, and surprise are good experiences. But that is already counted inside the welfare, so at the experience level variety should not be double counted. If two beings have the same valence, one from a very familiar experience and one from a novel one, then whatever the novelty adds is already inside the number, and something else in the familiar experience is making up the difference.

But the crux of Saturationism is not at the individual level but the pattern level. Elliott Thornley pressed this in his comment: "no one benefits from this variety. No one cares about this increased variety, at least in some sense of the word 'care.' You yourself, the person choosing Variety over Homogeneity, wouldn't care if you were incarnated into this universe." MacAskill answered: "The claim that Variety is better than Homogeneity is not a claim that each person in Variety is better off. It is a claim about the pattern of value in the world." I argue that the main mistake of this view sits exactly there. "The pattern of value in the world" invites us to count a fictional character's experience of variety, even though it could be that no individual experiences this variety at any moment in time.

The Reified Referent

In The Sexual Politics of Meat (1990), Carol J. Adams coined the absent referent: the animal is made to vanish from the meat, so that a living individual disappears behind a word. I propose the inverse operation, which I call the reified referent: language makes a nonentity appear inside the moral conversation and treats it as a stakeholder. The absent referent hides someone who is really there. The reified referent invents someone who is not there, at the expense, to a certain extent, of the individuals who are.

God is taken by some to be a case of this kind. If no god exists, then "we must do this because it pleases God" brings the preferences of a fictional character into ethics. The subtler cases are much harder to detect. A group made of you and your friend is real in the sense that its parts are real; the group as a collection is a useful thought experiment, but it has no patienthood of its own. A specific case of the reified referent happens when the group itself, or the "total picture", is quietly promoted from a collection of experiences to an experiencing subject who gets a vote.

There is a simple test: restate every value claim in terms of what some being feels or will feel. Whatever cannot be restated this way relies on a reified referent.

This is quite counterintuitive to me, but truth that is viewed as an intrinsic value is also a reified referent. I value truth enormously, but there is no God looking at the world and feeling happy when truth is revealed or reflected in it. Hence it should be viewed as of instrumental value.

Environmental ethics runs on this error, in my view. Intrinsic biodiversity value treats the diversity itself as mattering; the last rare lizard is said to matter intrinsically more than an individual of an abundant species. But no lizard knows he is endemic. The rarity is not in the lizard's life; it is in a catalog. The environmental language consistently hides the sentient and highlights the insentient, reified referents: "the ecosystem", "the species", "the balance of nature". But a forest full of color, valued apart from any mind watching it, is actually colorless. Color is not the wavelengths themselves. It appears when light meets a mind, which transforms signals from "outside", through the visual system from the retina to the brain, into something completely different in quality and essence. Without a mind, the beautiful picture is just waves and particles, and the forest is silent.

Two Sealed Rooms

Two beings live in sealed rooms. They will never meet, never learn of each other. In World V, being A spends an hour receiving a foot massage and being B eats a wonderful meal. In World H, both eat the wonderful meal. Every experience involved has exactly the same valence, the same quality level of goodness. Ask A whether she wants to switch worlds: she is indifferent, and she must be, because if she preferred one, the welfare would not be equal. Ask B, same answer, because nothing changes for him. No being, at any moment, in either world, is one drop better or worse off than in the other, yet the Saturation View holds that World V is better. "Better", though better for no one, is a sentence in search of a subject. The only way to make sense of it is to imagine a viewpoint hovering over both rooms, comparing the kinds of experiences, and preferring the spread. That viewpoint is the reified referent.

To count that look as a cost is to charge real beings for the boredom of a ghost. To view a being's joy as less worthy because of his species, or his location, or the fact that there are other beings with similar joys, seems equally mistaken to me.

Could Variety Push for More Suffering?

Variety is not the only pattern one could value. Think about spikes: a life where valence swings between very low and very high, against one with the same total welfare but a narrow, calm range.

Let's assume your total life's valence is just a bit above neutral. Within your life, you may prefer the spikes, which are more attuned to excitement, or the opposite, stable valence (tranquilism pushes further in that direction). I am more sympathetic to the latter. 

Spikes could be one parameter inside variety. If I get this right, stable valence does not leave much room for valence diversity, whereas spikes could give us, even under the same total valence and the same total equal valence for each individual, more variety of valence, hence of experience. This can lead us to a dangerous place where we push for a wider and wider spectrum of valence. I am especially worried about this since I value reducing suffering, especially the worst kinds, more than increasing happiness. A wider spectrum of valence is a bigger risk of severe suffering.

Why the Ghost Feels So Right

I argue that using a reified referent is a mistake, but it is a tempting one, and I have a few thoughts about why:

  • You cannot imagine an unwatched world without mentally watching it, or think about a world no one thinks about. But apart from individuals, almost by definition, no one is watching the world. I think it is better to see the world as the sum of experiences, nothing else. Any outside view, beyond individual experience, is not loyal to reality.
  • Homogeneity really does lower our welfare through boredom and diminishing returns, so we carry that feeling across lives, where it no longer applies. It is a bias.
  • No one proposes an ugly impersonal value. Diversity, beauty, complexity, wilderness: every impersonal value ever proposed is a pleasure to think about. If impersonal value were really independent of observers, that would be a strange coincidence. If impersonal values are observer pleasures projected onto a fictional observer, this is exactly what we should expect.

Is Pareto Using a Ghost Too?

When I claim a world with five suffering beings is worse than a world with three flourishing beings and two suffering ones, am I adopting a viewpoint nobody occupies? No individual experiences the sum. If the Totalist may hover above the world and add, why may the Saturationist not hover and compare types of experiences? One can argue that either both are ghosts or neither is.

This argument puzzles me, and I think there is something deeper here I am not able to put my finger on. 

I will say this: the summing view uses an imaginary accountant, yet that accountant only counts real things: valence, intensity, duration of consciousness, all of them properties present in the experience itself. Hence, the beings vote, and the accountant counts the votes. Under the Saturation View, the accountant votes: it discounts a joy according to a relation no one feels.

But what about inequality? Inequality is also a pattern that possibly no one feels. Imagine the two sealed rooms again: in world A the two someones have a positive welfare of 2 and 10, and in world B both have a welfare of 6. No one ever feels any inequality, so why should we prefer world B?

  • Compare the two worlds individual by individual, which I think is the right way to judge any situation, and the valence changes for every individual. If we push a button and switch from world A to world B, something meaningful happens to someone. This is not the case with the Saturation View, which could prefer one world over another where no individual is worse or better off, so pushing the button changes nothing for anyone.
  • If the signs were reversed and the numbers represented suffering, the value of reducing the most intense suffering would make us prefer world B.

Epilogue

The universe has no point of view. When we pretend it has one only in order to count what real beings really feel, I think that is a justifiable ethical move. When we let that pretend point of view vote, real beings pay the price. On the Saturation View there is always some point where real felt welfare should be sacrificed for an unfelt pattern: some being's day made worse so that the world looks better to no one. A civilization steering by this view is putting a lot of effort into decorating a gallery that has no visitors.

item.title: AI Alignment at Which Abstraction Level?
item.description:
This post is crossposted from my Substack, Structure and Guarantees, where I explore how formal verification and related ideas might scale to more complex intelligent systems. Here I start from the observation that AI alignment usually takes for granted a privileged role for human values, without asking why values should come from that particular abstraction level. I then give an independent engineering reason to worry about putting humans at the center of an alignment specification, drawing on lessons from formal verification at scale.

I’ve been arguing recently for a solution to the apparent chaos of current use of generative AI to write software: perhaps use these AI systems to help write truly unambiguous formal specifications, but then let those formal descriptions persist, auditing them carefully and using tools that reliably write code as we know it, given specifications. I made the case in one original article and then a follow-up responding to comments on the first. I ended the latter by promising to get into the highest-profile specification-writing challenge of our times: AI alignment. Here is the first of three articles giving my perspective.

First, I think a bit about my personal background is relevant. I have specialized in how to scale formal verification to apply to realistic systems without imposing unrealistic costs on engineers. Just to keep things interesting, I typically add another requirement: we want to minimize the trusted base of any given verification. In other words, imagine someone builds an artifact and formally verifies it. The trusted base includes every line of code where a bug could have led to accepting an artifact that actually doesn’t align with the author’s intent. We can find that the trusted base includes code of the artifact, say for the hardware if we have only proved software; code of the formal-verification tool, in the common case where it hasn’t itself been formally verified; or code of further infrastructure underneath either, like an operating system we trust to run the verification software. I’ll have plenty to say in later articles about the best practices of my community in this regard and how they may be helpful to seemingly new problems around AI.

The important upshot for now, though, is that my perspective is one of an engineer. My projects almost always involve building nontrivial artifacts alongside their machine-checked proofs. These are serious proofs checked into version control and often developed by multiple collaborating engineers. Little conceptual mistakes can lead to the proofs being rejected. It’s an activity that doesn’t seem to map well to mainstream AI-alignment work. On the one hand, we have best-effort projects to align and evaluate current AI models, without any particular theoretical guarantees. On the other hand, we have writing more in the register of philosophy (some to be cited shortly) that tackles the big questions of artificial general intelligence and how it may come about from recursive self-improvement. There are no rigorous proofs about complex implementations, because those implementations don’t exist yet or are diabolically unstructured in our present understanding and thus resistant to proof. As a result, it is easy to miss small conceptual problems that doom certain frameworks. I’m not saying I’ve pinpointed those problems! I just know from experience that the probability is near 100% that any complex system that hasn’t gone through rigorous formal verification is actually incorrect.

So let’s talk what makes for a good specification in the spirit of AI alignment, treated as part of a formal-methods project with familiar engineering considerations. By the way, I’m a newcomer to the world of alignment and will appreciate any dialogue about influential and related writing that I’ve missed. Our first stop in this article may seem like a bit of a swerve from the topic I just promised, but please bear with me. We will return to a formal-methods perspective on why we may not want to center humans in the top-level formulation of alignment, even if we play an important role internally.

Abstraction Layers of Life as We Know It

The field of AI alignment so far has generated some big and nonobvious ideas. What is called the value identification problem is basically figuring out the right specification for AI, from the perspective of some thinking agent that we want to privilege morally. The principle of complexity of value asserts that there is no short description of human values; there is fundamental complexity in what we have wound up wanting. This principle sounds like bad news for writing down human values as a formal specification! A well-known alternative proposal involves a kind of epistemic humility by advanced AIs, through the notion of coherent extrapolated volition (CEV). The idea is that the AI’s starting specification is that it should figure out what humans would really want, if they were augmented in certain ways. Then that derived specification should become primary.

The place where I get stuck is why we assumed centrality of humans in the value-identification problem, and I’ll explain two kinds of objections, in this section and the next, one philosophical and one grounded in the pragmatics of formal verification. These objections stand independently of each other.

I think it’s widely recognized in the field that formulating this CEV objective is very challenging, which certainly sounds right from a formal-methods perspective. Still, I run into an objection to it, even presuming perfect formalization of what it means to learn human preferences. The problem is potential conduct of an AI during the period when it is learning our preferences. Assume it doesn’t yet have perfect models of our behavior, so it can only learn through real observation of humans. What’s to stop it from putting us all in vats, Matrix-style, constantly running us through different VR scenarios, to most efficiently figure out our preference structure? Or, substantially less outlandishly, what’s to stop it from taking over our social-media feeds to try to provoke different emotions, learning our preferences at the same time as triggering social problems as we already see from infinite-scroll social media today? It’s not like we can assume some bootstrap morality that flags those tactics as unsavory; finding the bootstrap morality isn’t obviously an easier or different problem. Even if the AI eventually creates genuine paradise compatible with our values, we might object to the intervening dark ages of manipulation. (ChatGPT directed me to a recent paper by Emmons et al. studying a related problem more technically.) Now, it turns out that the rest of this section can proceed independently of this point, so I mostly include it in case readers have good references to share for prior art.

At some level, human centrality is obvious: humans are designing AI (for now), and humans want what we want. However, there is a familiar historical narrative of progress that depends on seeing ourselves as less and less central in the grand scheme of things. Copernicus argued that the Earth revolves around the Sun, not the other way around. Darwin argued that humans resulted from an evolutionary process that produced all of life as we know it, giving us no special place in the grand scheme of things. If we’re not a natural endpoint of a universal process, why should we give ourselves that status in the goals of powerful AI?

Bostrom in Superintelligence considers other approaches to indirect normativity, which try to avoid centering human values, but to me these formulations seem to run into trouble for assuming the major problem of specifying human morality is already solved, even if one formulation (“moral rightness”) is couched in terms of universal, not human, morality. I personally am convinced by moral anti-realism and see the case for universal morality as weak, as morality arises from evolutionary forces and should be expected to be different in different times and places.

My argument here is related to moral circle expansion, a philosophical concept that explains our potential granting of more moral standing to nonhuman animals and AIs alike. For instance, imagining our ancestors formulating alignment as recently as 150 years ago, it may have been “clear” that only a writer’s own race deserved consideration, a principle that we now find repugnant. We could perhaps say that I’m taking that principle to a more abstract level, where we see, say, humans and cows as representatives of roughly the same abstraction level of the universe, raising the question of what makes that level special.

Let’s consider the same question from more of an engineering perspective. Life can naturally be organized in layers, and we can imagine formulating alignment from the perspective of each layer, which can lead to very different outcomes via powerful AI systems, each outcome looking undesirable from other layers’ vantage points. What makes the layer of individual humans special – special enough to get this treatment in alignment?

I will have more to say on the biological version of this picture next time. I’m not, by the way, implying that atoms have human-style preferences. The point is more that it’s hard to formalize “preference” in some way that isn’t sneaking in a special role for humans. One common answer is that the organism layer is distinguished in supporting consciousness, but I’ve already argued against the big-picture utility of that word and won’t relitigate here.

One related alignment idea is natural abstraction: the idea that well-engineered thinking systems will develop the same abstractions for making sense of the vast physical world, because those abstractions just work, and thus we can assume that AI will evolve toward abstractions familiar to us, and we can specify alignment in terms of those abstractions without worry of (gross) misinterpretation. This perspective doesn’t tell us which of many abstractions to extract values from, though, including in situations as in the diagram with agents nested inside each other. That nesting also figures in the idea of embedded agency, which considers how agents should plan changes to complex worlds that include themselves. One subproblem is how agents should plan the creation of nested agents that do helpful supporting work. This perspective doesn’t seem to answer who deserves to be allowed to specify values: in the case of evolution optimizing humans who optimize Python programs, neither extreme orientation (toward highest-level or lowest-level optimizers) gives us the expected answer.

Engineers are used to thinking of systems at different levels of abstraction, and it’s jarring to call out one level as getting special treatment. Kurzweil in The Singularity is Near grounds the history of the universe in development of increasingly complex patterns, with nesting structure like I just sketched, but overloads the term “humanity” to cover whatever artificial intelligence we design, too. On one level, it solves the puzzle to decide that “human” is a synonym for the whole history of the universe, or at least the upcoming part for our own neighborhood in space! That move seems to me like hiding from the problem, though, if we think in terms of some greater cosmic destiny centered on forms of intelligence beyond our comprehension – and which, by the way, would be very helpful to us if they liked us.

Controlling Specification Complexity

Let’s snap back to the formal-methods engineer’s perspective. Whether we are formalizing human values directly or expressing what it means for a system to seek them out and then honor them, it sounds like one heck of a complex specification, and formal-methods people know that complex specifications create the biggest risk for assurance. Humans become an example of a complex legacy system, absolutely the worst kind to tackle for correctness-critical specifications. We evolved without selection pressure for our values to be understandable to computer code, so there’s no reason to think this problem is especially tractable. Maybe this problem is nonetheless the important one, and we just have to find a way to solve it, but let me continue explaining why it’s worrying (and then the next article will get into considering how the problem might actually be avoidable).

The trouble is that complexity in a specification tends to force complexity in an implementation, as code is added to deal with all the challenges that have been spelled out. Then, in turn, complexity of these two promotes complexity of a mathematical proof of correctness, which naturally references all parts of the specification and implementation. We may find that the specification includes N distinct concerns, and interaction among every pair of them (the feature interaction problem) needs to be treated explicitly in the proof, for N^2 required cases. This phenomenon should make us very wary to put a complex legacy system in the specification.

At this point, I’m imagining objections that sometimes we only know how to build systems including some complex parts. The usual saving grace for formal methods is the one I explained around surprising payoffs of end-to-end formal verification. Namely, sometimes it is easier to be sure we got a specification problem right by doing proof about a larger artifact that includes the original as one component. Why? The new top-level system may admit a simpler specification, and the original system’s specification becomes just part of internal implementation and proof details. If the inner system has a specification bug, either we catch it in the course of verifying the larger system or the bug turned out to be inconsequential for our larger goal.

Maybe the hard-to-decipher “humans” of the programming world are complex, popular programming languages like C. Assume for the moment (though I have argued to the contrary and will come back to doing so in later articles!) that building realistic computer systems requires using these programming languages. Are we out-of-luck, now needing to include formal semantics of the languages in our top-level system specifications? Not if we make the right architectural choices! If we also formally verify the implementations of the programming languages, then choice of language becomes an internal implementation detail, with no representation in the top-level specification that we should submit to careful auditing, testing, and so on. I presented one of my own projects that achieves as much, also crossing the hardware-software interface off the list of top-level specification complexities, by verifying the hardware, too.

Another great example from programming is memory safety. Here we are dealing with what is, in practice, a somewhat-nebulous property, governing how different pieces of code can share computer memory harmoniously, with clear rules for who is allowed to access what. Everyone knows C is not memory-safe, while Rust is memory-safe – but what does that statement really mean? We could try to put together a grand unifying theory of memory safety, but I argue that the real importance of memory safety is that it allows modular reasoning. That is, in the presence of memory safety, it is tractable to divide a program up into modules and give each one a separate specification and proof, without unreasonable interaction across the specifications, because we know modules won’t generally trash each others’ memory. Therefore, the mere ability to prove interesting behavioral theorems modularly demonstrates a desirable quality that subsumes what we really wanted from memory safety – and we avoided needing to define “memory safety” formally. (Incidentally, others have formalized a related intuition.) This observation is related to the one I wrote about where resistance to security vulnerabilities follows almost for free.

So, even if humans are central to the story for what constitutes AI alignment, it need not mean that the “top-level specification” of AI says anything about humans! Future AI systems could construct sophisticated models of humans, and the utility of those models to meet some ultimate goal could be proved from first principles, without putting those models in the trusted base. While we humans differ from programming languages in having evolved rather than been designed, the gap could perhaps be made up by formally verified AI scientists studying humans or whatever other relevant phenomenon, a topic I hope to return to in later articles.

Conclusion

Maybe we just won’t be smart enough to construct an initial specification of alignment that avoids bringing in complex modeling of humans, but I hope I’ve made some kind of case that it’s worth trying. I also want to reiterate that I’m using this article partly to get feedback about existing writing I should check out for its connections to (and potential poking of holes in) what I’ve written here. My next article will give one example of an approach to alignment that genuinely avoids including anything about humans in its top-level specification, while plausibly meeting our informal requirements for alignment. The last article in the trio will consider the infamous example of the paperclip maximizer and some potential mitigations against allowing one to develop.

item.title: The Forkmakers
item.description:
Imagine our civilization fell tomorrow. What would our descendants think of us? What would they know about the 21st century?

They would know surprisingly little about our greatest material triumphs. Our civilization’s favorite building materials aren’t made to last. Reinforced concrete only lasts a century; asphalt far less. Most of what we make out of steel will turn into a brownish oxidized dust in a few decades.

Information is even worse. The ancient Mesopotamians did their writing on clay tablets. Our knowledge is stored on hard drives, which die in a few years, or acidic paper, which dies in decades.

We do create things that will last. Glass (especially its shatter-resistant varieties), ceramics, stainless steel. 1000 years after the fall of our civilization, we will be known for one thing above all others: cutlery. Our heirs call us the Forkmakers.

What Survives a Thousand Years

Our civilization is large and powerful. We will leave lots of relics for the post-apocalypse. Coins, tires, aluminum cans. Vast landfills of disposable diapers. But all of that is useless. The most durable thing we make that our successors actually want to use is our silverware.

Cutlery is metal - thick metal. Anything designed to last a hundred runs in the dishwasher can withstand the elements. And we’ve made a lot of it. In this post-apocalyptic world, even the poorest peasant can afford to eat with a stainless steel fork.

The situation with plates is more complicated. Few natural processes can destroy them. But when the Forkmakers’ civilization died, they left many of their plates in wooden cupboards off the ground. The few survivors didn’t really prioritize safely removing the plates before the cupboards rotted, so billions of ceramic plates shattered in those dark decades. But somewhere like the Bay Area, which had a large and rich Forkmaker population, most middle-class families still have the ancestral Fiestaware.

And it’s fortunate they have the cookware of a more advanced civilization, because one of their plentiful foods - acorns - is difficult to prepare. But with enough resourcefulness and inherited forks, the people of the Bay Area enjoy a diet of acorns, wild oats, grapes and figs. They call themselves Oaklanders.

What about the rest of our metalwork? While stainless steel objects last forever, most other forms of steel rust away. The chassis of a car or the springs inside a mattress will be red dust before the first century is over.

Aluminum will be more interesting. After iron and steel, it’s the most important metal in the modern world.[1] It’s corrosion-resistant. Early scavengers looking for finished goods they can use will ignore decaying engine blocks and crushed soda cans in favor of our forks and knives. But as they move up the tech tree, the Oaklanders will start to see aluminum as a useful raw material. Aluminum melts more easily than bronze, and can be cast just as easily.[2] During humanity’s first rise, we didn’t learn to extract aluminum from ore until the 1880s. But with millions of tons of the stuff already extracted, the Oaklanders will have an Aluminum Age before their Bronze Age. For a shining moment, before easy aluminum reserves are exhausted, they could appreciate their ancestors for something besides forks.

A thousand years from now, they still have some of our glass.[3] Our phone screens survive, long after the rest of the phone is gone. They might be fun to play with; I imagine my distant descendants hunched over the glass screen ignoring their parents.

Windows and lightbulbs have mostly been smashed: either by time or by barbarian raiders from San Jose. Tempered glass - most of the windows of a car - is cooled non-uniformly, putting it under a constant pattern of stress and strain. This means if a car window breaks, the break spreads, turning it into gravel.

But tempered glass is tough. The future Bay Area has hundreds of thousands of car windows. Oaklander architecture allows for plenty of natural light, shining through glass from another civilization.

Interestingly, while conventional wisdom holds that the Forkmakers are responsible for glass, natural philosophers have long disagreed. They rolled their eyes at a ‘Forkmaker of the Gaps’ who can be invoked to explain any unexplained phenomenon. Eventually, large window quarries are discovered in what was once Southern California. Each one corresponds to a large concentration of forks. The scientific consensus on what the Forkmakers could do shifts.

So much for metal and glass. What about plastic? No individual piece of plastic will see as much usage as our forks and plates; plastic degrades too fast when exposed to UV light. But anyone digging through our cities will find literal tons of the stuff: mysterious shapeable substances that nobody knows how to replicate, that aren’t made by any known processes. Still, if you aren’t superstitious, you can just go into an old city or landfill and get more. There are countless plastics, but the Forkmakers conveniently stamped a little code on each of them. The plasticsmith is one of the most learned people in the village. He knows which plastics mix with what, and what their properties will be.

Plastic can be melted down by even a primitive culture, and reforged into something new. It’s lightweight, waterproof, and cheap. In the Bay Area, that mostly means cups, jugs, and buckets. But in rainier climates, homes will have plastic roofs.

It’s interesting to compare the roles of plastic and aluminum. Both are lightweight substances that are easy to work with. Both need advanced technology to produce, but were thrown far back in the tech tree by the fallen Forkmakers. Plastic and aluminum share many applications. Plastic actually melts at a lower temperature, and requires much less physical infrastructure to work with. But it comes in countless complicated varieties. And the fumes it gives off have the unfortunate tendency to kill off all but the most carefully tutored plasticsmiths before they reach the point of mastery. Today there are about five tons of plastic for every ton of aluminum, but the most easily accessible reserves will be degraded by UV radiation in a few decades. Whether the Plastic Age comes before or after the Aluminum Age depends on the details of the recovery: how quickly do the Oaklanders amass technological know-how versus material capital?

The Words of the Forkmakers

A thousand years from now, the Oaklanders are a powerful civilization. Recycling ancient plastic and aluminum is an important part of their economy, and they’ve even learned to work with steel, making our forks more valuable than ever.

But I don’t want to be remembered for my forks. Forkmaker society produced so much information: photographs, essays, newspapers, scientific journals. Unfortunately, the next thousand years aren’t going to be kind to the things we write on.

Digital information is toast. Even if this laptop was somehow preserved from the elements, even if someone could find electricity in the post-apocalypse, information on an SSD only lasts decades. CDs might last a little longer. But anything lasting a millennium is a deliberate stunt by an archivist, not a widespread storage technique that just happens to be millennium-rated. There are a thousand books carved in ceramic buried in a salt mine in Austria, and a couple thousand Rosetta disks (unreadable unless you have a microscope).

So digital is out. I’ve written millions of words in my life (and been the subject of trillions of bytes of espionage by tech companies). All of that is gone.

I’ve also been written about in a newspaper. But newspapers don’t last a thousand years. Paper, in general, doesn’t really last. It’s biodegradable and slightly acidic. Certain kinds of mites can eat it, water and fire both destroy it.

But we do have examples of paper-like things lasting a thousand years with nobody to take care of them. There are hundreds of thousands of pieces of papyrus that survived twice that long in the hot, dry desert of inland Egypt. There’s Roman writing on pressed wood as far north as England. There are thousand-year-old sutras written on paper - actual paper! - in a cave in China.


You can’t exactly curl up at night and read the Oxyrhynchus papyri: they’re too brittle. In the course of researching this piece, I learned that there are more types of paper than I had ever imagined, and their fates are at least as varied as the fates of our windows. Roughly speaking, paperbacks are all doomed. Hardcover books are printed on acid-free paper not unlike ancient papyrus. It’ll dry out, but if you take it to a humid environment, it might become bendable again. Glossy stock (think nice magazines) survives the best of all of these if you keep it dry. If it ever gets wet, though, mold will devour it, and it’s hard to stay dry for a thousand years anywhere on this planet.

What does it take for a library to last a millennium? It can’t be anywhere humid. Bad news, since we Forkmakers do most of our building on coasts. Nowhere with precipitation. Nowhere that will be inhabited at any point in the future: we humans have a nasty habit of burning each other’s cities to the ground.

But we Forkmakers live in many places. There are a hundred thousand libraries in the continental US,[4] ranging from elementary school collections to the Library of Congress. They’re built in every architectural style imaginable: many from the doomed mix of concrete and steel, some from wood or glass, but some from brick or stone. Many have archival stacks buried in basements. And, most important, some are in places that nobody- not a barbarian warlord, not a hunter-gatherer looking for kindling, not even a rat or termite, would ever think to venture. I’m talking about Las Vegas.[5]

The Lied Library at UNLV is perfect for preservation. The books are packed into metal bins the size of refrigerators. In our time, patrons can ask a robot to retrieve any title they wish. But fifty years from now, the bins will be buried under four stories of rubble. Many will be smashed when the building falls. But many will survive.

Imagine the excitement when an archeologist, digging in Las Vegas, discovers a university library. Millions upon millions of pages, more than she could read in a lifetime. She reaches out to touch one, and it crumbles to dust. But the Oaklanders are resourceful. Our heroine realizes that if they take the pages back to California, some become readable.

Well, readable is a generous term. In the time of the Forkmakers, there were only two major languages in North America: English and Spanish. A truly unprecedented amount of linguistic uniformity. After a thousand years, the Spanglish our Oaklander archeologist speaks is similar enough to English that if she had a modern recording, she could recognize the words, if not the grammar. Unfortunately, she doesn’t have a recording; she has writing. And English is a very hard language to read.

The breakthrough comes when she finds two different Forkmaker translations of the Bible. The Oaklanders have Bibles of their own and are able to decipher the strange writings of their forebears.

Understanding the text is the work of decades. The books are organized by size, fiction next to science next to self-help. There are scholarly debates about whether Elon Musk was a real person. There’s a scientific boom as Oaklander scholars work their way through the university library. But the greatest mystery of all is never answered: why do so few of the books talk about how to make a fork?

  1. ^

    Sorry, copper, no hard feelings

  2. ^

    At least if you alloy it with silicon, which the Forkmakers helpfully did.

  3. ^

    There’s a pernicious rumor going around that glass is a slow-flowing liquid. People sometimes justify this by pointing to old windows and noticing they’re uneven. By this logic, Roman glasswork couldn’t possibly have its incredible detail, and Neolithic obsidian arrowheads would be puddles by now.

  4. ^

    After a great deal of debate with Claude, I conceded that Canadian and Alaskan libraries are getting swallowed by fire- either natural or man-made- well before the millennium mark.

  5. ^

    The city was abandoned soon after the collapse, but its location was remembered by desert nomads for centuries. A thousand years from now, the Hoover Dam is still a tourist attraction; the Las Vegas ruins are for serious historians.

item.description:
TLDR; The New Critic, a gen z longform magazine on substack, is raising money to fund ambitious writing projects.

Hi LessWrong! I am one of the Founding Editors of The New Critic, and am writing to call attention to our Manifund campaign.

What is The New Critic:

The New Critic is a non-political, non-ideological magazine dedicated to developing extraordinary gen z writers and addressing the pressing questions of young people in the U.S. Our essays are primarily literary reportage, where we send a writer out into the world to meet their subjects, and then write about it. Our essays are free and we use Substack to meet readers where they are—on the internet.
